name: Ammisabad
title: Leader of the third month's military division under King David
summary: Ammishabad, son of Benaiah and grandson of the priest Jehoiada, commanded the third month's division in King David's rotating military system. The division consisted of 24,000 men, and Ammishabad held operational responsibility in his father's place, since Benaiah occupied a higher position in the king's service. David's kingdom was organized with twelve such divisions, each serving one month—a system that ensured continuous defense readiness while allowing soldiers to return home to their families and farms. Ammishabad's role reflects how military leadership in the united monarchy could be passed down within prominent families, testifying to the administrative sophistication under David's rule.

versions.summary: Ammisabad was the son of Benaiah and served as leader of the monthly military division in the third month under King David. He led a division of 24,000 men and was part of David's military organization as described in 1 Chronicles.
versions.title: Leader over David's military division
versions.reason: [minor] The title is functional but could be more precise. Ammishabad specifically led the third month's military division. A more accurate title would reflect this.; [major] Benaiah is referred to as 'high priest' in the title, which is incorrect. Benaiah (son of Jehoiada) was a warrior and military commander, not a high priest. The high priest Jehoiada is another person. The title must be corrected.; [minor] The description states that Benaiah was 'leader among the Thirty,' but more precisely, Benaiah was counted among the Thirty and placed over them; even more importantly, he led David's bodyguard (the Cherethites and Pelethites). The description should be clarified.; [minor] The phrasing "Ammishabad took over leadership after his father Benaiah" may give the impression that Benaiah was dead or retired. The text in 1 Chron 27:5-6 rather indicates that Benaiah was the chief leader and that his son Ammishabad led his division, possibly as a deputy. This nuance should be adjusted.; [minor] The summary is acceptable but could be improved with more context about the relationship between Benaiah and Ammishabad, and the role Ammishabad played as his father's deputy.; [minor] 'Warrior' is acceptable, but 'military commander' or 'army leader' would be more precise than simply 'warrior,' given that he led 24,000 men. The title 'division commander' could be considered.; [minor] There are no footnotes on interesting details. The name Ammishabad has an interesting etymology, and the context surrounding David's rotating military system deserves a historical/linguistic note.

versions.summary: Ammisabad was the son of Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, and served as leader of the monthly military division in the third month under King David. He led a division of 24,000 men and likely acted as a substitute for his father Benaiah, who was the original commander of this division. Ammisabad was part of David's well-organized military system with twelve rotating divisions, ensuring the kingdom's defense throughout the year.

versions.summary:
Ammishabad, son of Benaiah and grandson of Jehoiada, commanded the third month's division in King David's military system.  
The division consisted of 24,000 men, and Ammishabad served as its operational leader in place of his father, since Benaiah himself held a higher position in the king's service.  
David's kingdom was organized with twelve such rotating divisions, each serving one month per year—a system that ensured continuous defense of the realm while allowing soldiers to return home to their families and farms.  
Ammishabad's role shows that military leadership could be inherited, and that Benaiah's family held a prominent position in the power structure of the united kingdom.

footnotes.text: The name Ammisabad (Hebrew: עַמִּיזָבָד, 'Ammizabad') likely means 'my people have given' or 'the generous kinsman'. The Hebrew element 'am' (עַם) means 'people' or 'kinsfolk', while 'zabad' (זָבָד) means 'to give' or 'gift'. The name follows a common Semitic naming tradition where family relationships are combined with a divine or human action.

David's system of twelve rotating army divisions, where each division of 24,000 men served one month per year, represented a sophisticated military organization. The total force of 288,000 men ensured continuous military readiness while allowing soldiers to return to agriculture and family during the other months. Similar rotation systems are known from other ancient kingdoms in the Middle East.

Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was one of David's most prominent warriors and later became commander-in-chief of Solomon's army. The fact that his son Ammishabad took over operational leadership of the third month's division illustrates how military positions in the united kingdom could be inherited within prominent families.

Archaeological finds from the Iron Age in Israel and Judah, including fortifications and administrative ostraca, support the picture of a centralized state administration under David and Solomon. Although the exact size of the army divisions is debated among scholars—the Hebrew word 'elef' can mean both 'thousand' and 'military unit'—the system testifies to an organized military structure.

In the theological context of Chronicles, David's kingdom is emphasized as a well-ordered, God-given institution. The detailed listing of military leaders, including Ammishabad, serves to show that the kingdom was governed with wisdom and order—an ideal that the chronicler presents as a model for the post-exilic community.
